Alex Wroblewski | Afp | Getty Images U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday to "be careful" in public statements about U.S. support for Ukraine . U.S.-provided Starlink internet was recently restricted in Ukraine, hindering the war-torn country's ability to respond to Russian assaults. Ukraine uses Starshield, the military and government-controlled version of the commercial Starlink, to conduct military operations. In an earlier interview on NBC's "Meet the Press," Zelenskyy said he believed the U.S. government was responsible for the slowdown, and that Ukraine was "blocked" from U.S. intelligence for a period of time. Zelenskyy said Starshield-linked vehicles and drones are still being restricted in speed. Read more CNBC politics and policy coverage Trump waives broad new Russia sanctions and tariffs under Graham Act 2026 midterms money race: Democrats surge as Musk backs Republicans Why Trump and GOP's billion-dollar midterm election blitz isn't working Bessent cautioned Zelenskyy about making those claims. "President [Donald] Trump and Secretary [Marco] Rubio have categorically said that no one under the Trump administration did that, and I think it is very reckless for President Zelenskyy to make such a charge," Bessent said on "Meet the Press." "President Zelenskyy should be very careful about making statements like this that aren't true," he added. Starlink, high-speed satellite internet provided by Elon Musk's SpaceX , is critical to Ukraine's defense. Musk himself said in a post on X last week that the U.S. government and President Donald Trump are "ultimately" responsible for any slowdowns to the military version of Starlink known as Starshield . "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government," Musk wrote. "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS." Reuters reported last week that the White House ordered the technology restrictions, but Trump has denied responsibility for the slowdown. "Well, I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," the president said last week. "And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been." The U.S. relationship with Ukraine has been highly scrutinized throughout Trump's second term, as he has frequently antagonized the war-torn country while pushing for a peace deal. Trump has recently expressed frustration over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries as he faces pressure from voters over sky-high gasoline and diesel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections. The president has even personally blamed Zelenskyy for the rise in energy prices: "He wants to make problems for the world. He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel," Trump said. Soaring energy prices are largely due to the U.S. war with Iran, which severely disrupted the Strait of Hormuz and choked oil shipments from the Persian Gulf. The national average for a gallon of gas in the U.S. was nearly $4.30 on Sunday, according to AAA . Diesel was roughly $6.32 per gallon, about 20 cents off September's record high. Trump has tried to offset the energy pinch by importing Russian diesel. In a post on Truth Social earlier in the month, he said: "Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" Many U.S. lawmakers, including Republicans, have condemned the president's plan to buy Russian diesel. Congress recently sent Trump an overwhelmingly bipartisan sanctions package aimed at crippling Russia's energy industry. Trump signed the bill into law, but waived portions of it over the weekend, citing the national interest in an explanation to Congress. "Beyond irresponsible. What part of enforcing a law passed 86-11 by the Senate does the President and his advisors not understand?" Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said in a post on X . "It's unconscionable that this administration is capitulating to a Russian dictator who illegally invaded Ukraine and butchers innocent civilians every single day." headlines.title: Always on, always listening: New AI devices are pushing legal limits and could put users in jeopardy
headlines.summary: AI always-listening wearables from Apple, Amazon, Meta and other startups are getting creative with privacy rules and fueling concerns about covert recordings.
headlines.article_text: New AI wearables push the limits of privacy and wiretap laws Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Apple, Amazon, Meta and a host of startups have released AI-powered, always-listening devices this year. Unlike earlier smart speakers that were activated with a "wake word," these devices are pushing the limits of privacy law in new ways. In some states, experts say the legal exposure may fall on the person wearing the device during a private conversation without the required consent from bystanders. In this article AMZN META AAPL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT A titanium Apple Watch Ultra 4 during a product unveiling event at Apple Park in Cupertino, California, US, on Wednesday, Sept. 9, 2026. David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty Images Chris Thomas is all-in on AI gadgets. Thomas, 43, wears a pair of Meta 's camera-equipped glasses, a Fieldy note-taking pendant around his neck and a wristband from Amazon 's Bee, all of which record his daily life. A Pittsburgh-based business owner and a livestreamer, Thomas relies on the devices to help him stay organized, pay bills on time and set reminders. "I'm forgetful AF," Thomas said in an interview. "My life is so crazy that not having to remember to remember is fantastic." Not everyone is on board with his lifestyle. Earlier this week, a bystander at a local bar noticed his Meta Glasses. "He was like, 'I don't feel comfortable,'" Thomas said. "I don't turn it off, I take it off completely because people don't really believe it's off." It's the type of interaction users are increasingly navigating as more tech companies introduce AI-powered, always-listening devices and features, which have been marketed as useful tools to transcribe meetings, keep track of conversations, set reminders and offer personalized recommendations. The latest example of these gadgets arrived Thursday with Amazon's Bee Frontier wearable and Bee Eclipse, a card-shaped device that attaches to a smartphone. Both devices are designed to record, transcribe and analyze a user's day. Amazon's Bee Frontier device can be worn on a wrist or clipped on to clothing. Amazon Apple's latest Apple Watch Series 12, unveiled in September, will have Siri Recap, which "ambiently" takes notes throughout the day and generates summaries of conversations. Another feature called Live Rewind can recap 15 seconds of a conversation via a text transcription. Meta's popular smart glasses can take photos, capture video and record voice notes or reminders. Startups including Plaud and Pocket also developed card-sized note-taking devices, while Friend offers an AI necklace. The devices have fueled concerns that they could erode privacy, by enabling covert recording without obtaining bystanders' consent and collecting sensitive data that's potentially accessible to others. Amazon, Google and other makers of voice-activated smart speakers faced similar privacy concerns when their devices first hit the market, in some cases leading to lawsuits and regulatory fines. But this new generation of AI devices is also testing the limits of privacy law. Unlike earlier smart speakers that were activated via a so-called "wake word" and sometimes stored recordings or sent audio to the cloud, some of these products can continuously listen, interpret speech, and extract its meaning without retaining the underlying audio. This capability has raised a largely untested question about whether that processing itself can amount to an unlawful interception. "With new technology like this, my statement is always to embrace with caution," Karen Panetta, dean of graduate education at Tufts' School of Engineering and a fellow at the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, said. She added, "If I'm giving permission for myself to be recorded, or for everything I look at to be recorded, that doesn't mean everybody else around you has given that consent." watch now VIDEO 1:33 01:33 Apple makes its biggest smart-home push yet under CEO John Ternus Squawk Box Asia The gray area Apple and Amazon appear to have sidestepped some of the privacy concerns that dogged earlier voice assistants. Apple says the feature does not store audio, send recordings to its servers, or involve human review. Amazon has said it doesn't store audio from Bee devices, and conversations are processed in a secure environment "where no one, including Amazon, can access your data." But that may not resolve the legal question. Many state wiretap and eavesdropping laws are written around whether a private communication was intercepted or its contents were acquired — not simply whether a conventional audio recording was created. Colin Zick, a privacy and data security attorney at Foley Hoag, said Apple appears to have learned from the first wave of litigation over voice assistants. But the new technology raises questions those earlier cases never had to answer: Can a system that is continuously listening, interpreting speech and turning it into a summary still amount to an interception if it never saves the underlying audio? Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg wears the Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses, as he delivers a speech presenting the new line of smart glasses, during the Meta Connect event at the company's headquarters in Menlo Park, California, U.S., Sept. 17, 2025. Carlos Barria | Reuters Some state laws define interception broadly. Massachusetts, for example, defines an intercepting device to include equipment capable of "transmitting, receiving, amplifying, or recording" a communication, while the "contents" of a communication can include its substance and meaning. In Zick's view, a device that continuously receives speech and produces a written summary could potentially fall within that language even without retaining an audio file. And in some states, the bigger legal risk may fall not on Apple, Amazon or other AI gadget makers but on the person wearing the device. "A non-wearer did not buy the watch, agree to Apple's terms, or choose to have their conversation summarized in the app," Zick said. The law covers not only recordings, but the "aural or other acquisition" of the contents of a communication. That could create an unusual situation in which an ordinary consumer turns on a feature built into a mainstream device and, at least technically, runs afoul of state law by using it during a private conversation without everyone's consent. Pi said a user in New Hampshire could potentially face civil or criminal liability for doing so, though he stressed that the practical risk of prosecution is far lower. It could be difficult to know whether someone had the feature enabled in the first place, and he said he would be surprised to see prosecutors pursue cases involving a bare statutory violation where no one was harmed. The legal questions are also different from those raised by earlier smart speakers and voice assistants. Those cases often centered on devices mistakenly activating or capturing speech that was not intended as a command. Here, the feature is designed to acquire and interpret the substance of a conversation — and the user has deliberately opted in. The string of sharp questions, some from voters who said they had supported him and President Donald Trump , previewed the rocky path he may face if he runs for president in 2028 and has to answer for the administration's record. Vance, who said during the town hall there's "of course" a chance he doesn't run for president, faced an especially pointed question about "a failure of leadership" posted by the widow of one of six U.S. soldiers killed by an Iranian drone strike in Kuwait, which occurred the day after Trump started the war with Iran. "This literally is the first time I've heard of this," Vance said in response. As he went on, he said, "This job is an amazing honor, but you live in a bit of a bubble and sometimes information doesn't filter up." Iran war strategy and costs After telling the vice president about his late wife, Master Sgt. Nicole Amor, who was killed on March 1, Joey Amor asked about mistakes and fundamental failures that led up to the deaths of those soldiers and how leaders would be held accountable. Vance seemed taken aback by Amor's questions, saying, "This literally is the first time I've heard of this," and said he wanted to talk with Amor afterward to learn more. But as Vance went on, he acknowledged mistakes were made and said, "There were issues with where troops were located that we realized was a huge mistake that we could do better on, and we have changed that." A Michigan man who said he voted for Trump and Vance in 2024 but now plans to vote for Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed pressed Vance about the high gasoline prices resulting from the war. In response, Vance said he recognized that gas prices were too high, and said, "I think it's important to be honest about why they're so elevated." He said it was because of "what's happening in the Middle East" and that the administration was taking steps to lower prices. "We've never had a situation like this where you have effectively the largest state sponsor of terrorism that's trying to choke off world energy supply," Vance said, without acknowledging that situation occurred because of the war Trump launched. He also blamed former President Joe Biden , saying that during his tenure, America's refining capacity was diminished. But when Vance was pressed on whether the Trump administration owned the current situation, the vice president suggested that looking backward for blame wasn't the way. "Fundamentally, we are where we are, and you have to, in my view, I'd like to know what is Abdul El-Sayed's solution for the problem that we have right now," Vance said. "It's easy to criticize something that happened seven months ago." Immigration enforcement tactics and rhetoric A nun who spoke to Vance about their shared Catholic faith questioned the administration's hardline immigration enforcement tactics, including children who are separated from their parents when the adults are swept up in sweeps, and how that squared with their values. "We're trying to strike the right balance," Vance said. When moderator Tony Dokoupil asked Vance if the administration is not striking that balance, Vance replied, "I think that is constantly a work in progress." He admitted that, "Sometimes you have some people who made mistakes. Sometimes you have some people who really screw up." When Dokoupil asked for specific examples, Vance said the administration has investigated several cases that resulted in further training or discipline for immigration enforcement officers, but they don't advertise them publicly to let investigations play out. Another voter, who said she became an immigrant five years ago and voted for Vance after becoming a U.S. citizen, asked him pointedly about his recent remarks referring to H1-B visa holders as "foreign indentured servants," and accused him of "scapegoating immigrants for the issues you're supposed to be solving." "To the extent that my rhetoric has been imperfect here, that's on me," Vance said, before explaining that he was trying to criticize the companies that bring in the workers, not the immigrant workers themselves. Selling access to White House 'disgusting and despicable' Dokoupil pressed Vance on whether Trump and others in his administration profited from the presidency, including the nearly $1.2 billion the president took in from his crypto businesses last year, according to a federal filing. When asked if he'd seen anything in the White House that made him squeamish, Vance said, "I've never seen anything like that from the president." He said, though, that there is evidence of corruption in Washington, but he doesn't see evidence of it from the president or the administration. Vance said he's read articles about allegations, but he investigates claims himself and finds they are not true. Dokoupil asked Vance about the president's crypto profits, as well as the recent resignation of his ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle, over allegations she denies that she leveraged her position for benefits. "If somebody's selling access to the White House, that's disgusting and despicable, and they should suffer consequences," Vance said.
